cards.front: Why prefer PreparedStatement to Statement?
cards.back: It is precompiled and parameterised — faster on reuse, and safe from SQL injection
cards.extra: The parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so a value can never be parsed as SQL syntax.

cards.front: How do you call a stored procedure from JDBC?
cards.back: With CallableStatement, prepared as {call proc(?, ?)}
cards.extra: Register output parameters with registerOutParameter before executing.

cards.front: What does ResultSet represent, and how do you iterate it?
cards.back: A cursor over the query result; while (rs.next()) advances one row
cards.extra: Read columns by index or name; next() returns false at the end. Always close it.

cards.front: What is a JDBC batch update for?
cards.back: Sending many statements in one round trip: addBatch() then executeBatch()
cards.extra: Inserting 10,000 rows one at a time is dominated by network latency, not by the database.

cards.front: How do you run several statements as one transaction in JDBC?
cards.back: Turn off auto-commit, then commit() or rollback()
cards.extra: conn.setAutoCommit(false) begins the transaction implicitly; the connection controls the boundary, not the SQL.

cards.front: What is DatabaseMetaData for?
cards.back: Discovering the database's capabilities and schema: tables, columns, driver version, supported features
cards.extra: The portable way to inspect a database without vendor-specific SQL.

cards.front: What are the four JDBC driver types?
cards.back: Type 1 bridge (JDBC-ODBC), Type 2 native API, Type 3 middleware, Type 4 pure Java
cards.extra: Type 4 is what every modern driver is: it speaks the database's wire protocol directly, no native code.

cards.front: What is Connection in JDBC?
cards.back: A session with the database, from which you create statements
cards.extra: It is the unit of transaction scope. Connections are expensive — that is why pool is a thing.

cards.front: What are the four pieces of the java.util.logging architecture?
cards.back: Logger (API), Handler (destination), Formatter (layout), Filter (accept/reject)
cards.extra: A Logger passes a LogRecord to its handlers; each handler formats and filters it independently.

cards.front: What are JUL's log levels, in increasing severity?
cards.back: FINEST, FINER, FINE, CONFIG, INFO, WARNING, SEVERE
cards.extra: There are also the aliases ALL and OFF for configuring threshold. FINEST is the most verbose.

cards.front: Why is the logger name usually the class name?
cards.back: Loggers form a hierarchy by dotted name, so configuration and levels are inherited from parents
cards.extra: com.example.Shop inherits the settings of com.example — that is why "set com.example to FINE" works.

cards.front: What does a Handler do?
cards.back: Delivers a LogRecord to a destination: console, file, socket, memory
cards.extra: ConsoleHandler, FileHandler. A logger can have several, each with its own level and formatter.

cards.front: What is LogRecord?
cards.back: The object carrying one log event: level, message, timestamp, source class and method, thrown exception
cards.extra: It is the single object that travels from the Logger through every Handler and Filter, carrying the level, message, timestamp, source class/method and the thrown exception.

cards.front: What does LogManager do?
cards.back: Owns the logger hierarchy and reads the logging configuration file
cards.extra: You rarely touch it; it is how the configuration is loaded at startup.

cards.front: What is the ObjectMapper in Jackson?
cards.back: The main entry point: converts Java objects to JSON and back
cards.extra: writeValueAsString, readValue. It is thread-safe once configured, so build one and share it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What is JsonNode in Jackson?
cards.back: A JSON document held as a tree you can navigate and modify
cards.extra: For when the shape is not known ahead of time, or you only need a couple of fields.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: When would you use Jackson's JsonParser instead of ObjectMapper?
cards.back: For streaming very large documents where you do not want the whole tree in memory
cards.extra: It is the low-level token API; the ObjectMapper is built on it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What is Gson, and how does it differ from Jackson?
cards.back: Google's JSON library, also object-to-JSON mapping
cards.extra: Same job, fewer features. It is still common in Android and legacy code.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What are the three Java XML parsing approaches?
cards.back: DOM (tree in memory), SAX (streaming push callbacks), StAX (streaming pull)
cards.extra: DOM for manipulation, SAX for large documents you only read, StAX when you want to drive the loop yourself.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What is the cost of DOM?
cards.back: The whole document is built in memory as a node graph
cards.extra: Convenient for editing and XPath, impossible for a 2 GB file.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: How does SAX work?
cards.back: You register a handler and the parser calls it for each event: start element, characters, end element
cards.extra: Push model; no tree, no memory cost. DefaultHandler is the base class you extend.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What is the key difference between SAX and StAX?
cards.back: SAX pushes events at you; StAX lets you pull them one at a time
cards.extra: Pull parsing composes better: you can stop early, or hand the reader to another component.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What are StAX's two APIs?
cards.back: Cursor API (XMLStreamReader) and Iterator API (XMLEventReader)
cards.extra: The cursor is faster and lighter; the event iterator is nicer to read and allows peeking.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::12 JSON and XML

cards.front: What is the difference between Pattern and Matcher?
cards.back: Pattern is the compiled regex (immutable, reusable); Matcher is one match attempt over one input
cards.extra: Compile once, then create a matcher per input — compiling in a loop is a common performance bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::06 Regular Expressions

cards.front: Which Matcher method requires a full match?
cards.back: matches() — the whole input must match the pattern
cards.extra: find() searches for a match anywhere, and lookingAt() anchors at the start only.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::06 Regular Expressions

cards.front: How do you read captured groups?
cards.back: group(n) after a successful match; group 0 is the whole match
cards.extra: groupCount() tells you how many groups exist. Named groups are (?<name>...) and read with group("name").
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::06 Regular Expressions
